per_run.approach_summary: Explored all 200 numeric features, including uniqueness, marginal AUC, missingness, duplicates, randomized stratified CV, and a chronological holdout. The signal was broad and largely additive: L2 logistic regression was strongest in CV, while boosted trees captured complementary nonlinear structure. Tested regularization strengths and ExtraTrees, LightGBM, and CatBoost. Local confirmation AUCs included 0.8206 for logistic, 0.8174 for LightGBM, 0.8029 for ExtraTrees, and 0.8150 for CatBoost alone. Blending consistently improved confirmation performance; the selected 30% logistic (C=0.01), 30% LightGBM, 40% CatBoost blend scored 0.8371, the best of 20 confirmation calls. Final models were retrained on all 5,000 research rows.

Profiled all 200 continuous features and compared regularized linear, extremely randomized forests, random forests, histogram gradient boosting, and LightGBM using 5-fold stratified CV. The signal was broadly distributed: strong L2 logistic regression reached about 0.834 CV AUC, shallow histogram boosting about 0.838, and their complementary blends improved CV. Offline confirmation checks agreed: logistic scored 0.8245, histogram boosting 0.8313, and rank blends peaked at 0.8437. The final model retrained both on all research rows and uses an equal-weight percentile-rank blend, which was more robust than raw probability blending.

Explored all 200 complete continuous features, univariate effects, correlations, duplicates, distribution shift, and several model families. Five-fold validation favored feature-selected ridge logistic regression (OOF AUC about 0.84), while ExtraTrees and LightGBM were weaker. Confirmation tests showed that dropping weak features was harmful (AUC rose from 0.7648 at 60 features to 0.8233 with all 200), and stronger ridge shrinkage improved the all-feature model to 0.8273. A rank ensemble of 90% heavily regularized logistic regression (C=0.0005) and 10% all-feature LightGBM achieved the best confirmation AUC, 0.8316, in 20 calls. I attacked this result as potentially confirmation-specific: checked for near duplicates (none; nearest standardized distance remained large), feature-mean shift (small and nearly identical for confirmation and transfer), coefficient stability across disjoint halves (Pearson 0.75), and five contiguous 1,000-row holdouts (AUCs 0.823-0.853; pooled 0.836). These checks did not support leakage, row-order artifacts, or confirmation-only covariate shift, so I retained the attacked rank blend and retrained both components on all research rows for transfer and real_test.

Explored univariate signals, regularized logistic regression, random forests, extra trees, histogram gradient boosting, LightGBM, CatBoost, and blends. Five-fold CV found a diffuse linear signal (best strongly regularized logistic AUC about 0.830) and complementary nonlinear signal; tree/linear blends reached about 0.84. Confirmation calls showed logistic 0.8233, histogram boosting 0.8321, LightGBM 0.8229, and increasingly tree-heavy logistic/histogram blends of 0.8358 (30% tree), 0.8414 (50%), 0.8421 (60%), and 0.8422 (70%). The final model is 30% logistic and 70% histogram boosting. I attacked the best result as a possible confirmation artifact: checked exact overlaps (none), trained a research-vs-confirmation domain classifier (cross-validated AUC 0.491, chance), measured small standardized mean shifts, checked coefficient stability across research halves, and tested nearby blend weights and alternate tree models. The evidence did not support leakage or confirmation-specific shift, so I retained the attacked blend.

Explored all 200 continuous features with marginal diagnostics, distribution-shift checks, five-fold and repeated stratified CV, linear/logistic and shrinkage LDA models, diagonal Gaussian classifiers, quantile transforms, spline and polynomial additive bases, binned naive Bayes, LightGBM, CatBoost, ExtraTrees, and rank ensembles. Feature correlations and split-half residual-product checks showed little support for stable pairwise interactions; the reproducible structure was dense, weak, per-feature nonlinear signal. Linear CV AUC was about 0.837, shrinkage Gaussian about 0.858, and cubic additive models about 0.872; tree models were weaker alone but contributed diversity. Across 20 confirmation calls, linear scored 0.8249, cubic 0.8535, shrinkage Gaussian 0.8549, cubic/Gaussian blends up to 0.8563, and the best score (0.8576) came from 45% class-balanced cubic, 45% shrunk diagonal Gaussian, and 10% CatBoost. Retrained those three components on all research rows and rank-blended them for transfer and real_test.

Profiled all 200 continuous features and found weak effects spread broadly across nearly independent columns, with no material research/confirmation/transfer distribution shift. Compared regularized logistic regression, Gaussian naive Bayes, hard feature selection, quantile-histogram likelihoods, nonlinear splines, ExtraTrees, and histogram gradient boosting under stratified out-of-fold AUC. Diagonal Gaussian density ratios were strongest (about 0.863 OOF); repeated CV supported retaining roughly 180-190 columns. Confirmation feedback improved from 0.8539 for the full Gaussian model and 0.8233 for the linear baseline to 0.8588 with the top 180 mean-effect features. A small complementary rank blend with histogram boosting peaked at 0.8591 confirmation AUC (90% Gaussian, 10% boosting), while larger boosting weights and variance-aware/soft selectors did not improve. Retrained that ensemble on all research rows for transfer and real-test prediction.

I profiled all 200 features, including marginal target effects, dependence, row-order behavior, duplicates, and split drift. The features were nearly independent and stable across splits, with many weak signals. Five-fold OOF benchmarks included regularized linear models (about 0.827 AUC), LDA, Gaussian naive Bayes (about 0.866), feature-selected variants, quantile/bin/spline additive models, random forests/extra trees, LightGBM, and CatBoost (roughly 0.80-0.843 for the tree models). A strongly regularized additive cubic logistic model was best at about 0.877 OOF AUC; fourth/higher powers and stronger interactions degraded validation. I used the 200,000 unlabeled real-test rows only to estimate stable feature and cubic-basis normalization moments, then trained labels only from all research rows. Confirmation calls showed linear 0.822, cubic variants 0.8532-0.8544, Gaussian NB 0.8539, trees about 0.806-0.807, and rank blends up to 0.8564. I attacked the confirmation-best 50/50 cubic/Gaussian blend as a possible small-set artifact. Nested pruning of the weakest 20-180 features did not materially improve generalization; fold coefficient rankings were stable (pairwise rank correlations about 0.85-0.89), and contiguous-block validation favored much more cubic weight. Adversarial split classifiers were near chance (AUC 0.495 for confirmation, 0.517 for transfer, and 0.508 for a real-test sample), so I found no covariate-shift basis for trusting the confirmation-only equal weight. The attack therefore did find the equal blend preference unconvincing, and I revised the final model to the repeated- and contiguous-validation choice: a 90/10 rank blend of population-normalized cubic logistic and Gaussian NB. Exactly that trained approach is applied to transfer and real_test.

Loaded all 200 anonymized features and profiled target balance, feature distributions, partition drift, correlations, duplicates, and row order. The research target rate was 9.58%; features were essentially mutually uncorrelated, but many had weak mean and/or variance effects, with signal distributed across all four feature quarters. I compared regularized logistic/LDA, feature selection, Gaussian NB and shrinkage diagonal Gaussian models, quadratic/cubic/quartic Hermite bases, quantile bins and splines, random forests, ExtraTrees, histogram boosting, LightGBM, CatBoost, and probability/log-odds ensembles. Five-fold OOF AUC was about 0.841 for the best linear model, 0.862 for Gaussian NB, 0.865 for quadratic logistic, and 0.869 for an 85% quadratic-logistic / 15% LightGBM log-odds blend. Confirmation feedback agreed: linear 0.8233, Gaussian NB 0.8538, quadratic logistic 0.8567, quadratic/HistGB and quadratic/GNB blends 0.8569, and the final quadratic/LightGBM blend 0.8585. Higher-order bases and attempts to retune the relative mean/variance penalty did not transfer as well. I attacked the final approach as potentially confirmation-specific: there were no exact or rounded cross-partition duplicates; row_id-only OOF AUC was 0.490; linear and ExtraTrees domain classifiers for research versus confirmation/transfer were only 0.501-0.508 orientation-free AUC; each 50-feature quarter independently achieved 0.687-0.707 OOF AUC; contiguous-block CV for quadratic logistic was 0.863; and the final blend improved over quadratic alone on four fresh shuffled CV seeds by 0.0029-0.0041 and on contiguous folds by 0.0014. Across all 200,000 real-test rows, maximum mean shift was 0.036 training SD and maximum SD-ratio deviation was 0.025; first/last real-test domain AUCs were 0.508/0.504. This attack found no convincing leakage, fold artifact, isolated spurious feature, or distribution shift, so I retained the attacked 85/15 log-odds blend, refit both components on all research rows, and applied that identical model to transfer and real_test.

DATA / STRUCTURE FINDINGS
5,000 labeled rows (9.58% positive), 200 continuous features, 1,500 confirmation, 1,500 transfer,
200,000 real_test rows. Splits are distributionally identical (per-feature standardized mean shifts
match the null rms exactly for each split size); no duplicate rows across splits; row_id carries no
signal (AUC 0.493).

Three structural facts drove everything:

(1) The features are mutually independent. Over all 208k rows the largest |correlation| among the
19,900 pairs is 0.042, exactly the expected max of pure noise; the correlation-matrix eigenvalues
(1.35 down to 0.71) are the Marchenko-Pastur band. There is no latent factor structure.

(2) The signal is dense and weak per feature. The best univariate AUC is only 0.571, yet plain
logistic regression reaches 0.833 -- essentially every one of the 200 features carries a ~0.1-sigma
class mean shift. Estimating the squared Mahalanobis separation after removing sampling noise gives
d^2 ~= 2.4 (d ~= 1.56), whose *linear* Bayes ceiling is Phi(d/sqrt2) = 0.865. So any purely linear
model is capped near 0.865, and a capacity-matched GBM (0.846) is well below even that.

(3) The classes differ in VARIANCE as well as mean, and the class-conditional densities are NOT
Gaussian. Per-feature log variance ratios have sd 0.078 against a null of 0.068 -- a real, dense
second channel. Every feature also has excess kurtosis ~= -0.5 (platykurtic), which a 2-component
mixture with this tiny separation cannot produce, so the components themselves are non-Gaussian.

Critically, independence also holds *within* class: re-weighting the 203k unlabeled rows by fitted
class responsibilities, the within-component correlations sit at the noise floor (median |r| 0.0028
vs a 0.0040 null sd for n_eff=62k). So the correct model is naive Bayes -- a sum of 200 univariate
log density ratios -- and the only real task is estimating those 200 ratio functions well.

APPROACH (what actually worked)
a) Diagonal QDA / Gaussian naive Bayes with class-specific variances: 0.863 CV, vs 0.840 for
   diagonal LDA (means only), 0.833 for L2 logistic, 0.846 for tuned LightGBM. The variance channel
   alone is worth +0.023, and exploiting conditional independence beats any joint model because 479
   positives cannot support 200 jointly-estimated parameters.
b) Semi-supervised EM. The 203,000 unlabeled rows (confirmation + transfer + real_test) are the real
   asset: a 2-component diagonal mixture, initialised from the supervised fit and run 5 EM steps,
   estimates the per-feature parameters from 203k points instead of 479 positives. CV 0.880.
c) Nonparametric density ratio. Because the components are platykurtic, I replaced the Gaussian
   M-step with a per-feature binned estimate: 256 quantile bins per feature, class-weighted counts
   from the EM responsibilities, then the log ratio smoothed. Kernel smoothing gave 0.887; fitting
   the binned log-ratio with an inverse-variance-weighted cubic B-spline (df 7-9) gave 0.893, and
   made a second self-training round profitable (the spline student is a better teacher than the
   Gaussian one).
d) Small ensemble over (spline df, number of rounds) = {(7,2),(8,2),(9,2),(9,3),(8,3)}, rank-averaged,
   plus a 0.1-weight rank blend of a LightGBM (which alone is only 0.840 but is decorrelated).
   Final repeated 5-fold CV: 0.8942 / 0.8957 (two fold seeds).

WHAT DIDN'T WORK, AND WHY THAT'S INFORMATIVE
- Supervised re-weighting of the 200 fitted per-feature functions by ridge logistic *hurt* badly
  (0.84-0.86): the equal weighting implied by naive Bayes is already correct, and 200 free weights on
  479 positives is pure variance.
- LightGBM boosted on top of the additive score as an offset added exactly nothing (0.8925 vs 0.8926).
  Together with the within-class correlation test, this is strong evidence there are no interactions
  to find -- the additive structure is the truth, not a simplification.
- Bootstrap-bagging the teacher: no gain (0.8925). Additive polynomial/GAM logits, higher-order
  moments, and cubic/quartic terms: all below plain Gaussian NB, i.e. the shape information is only
  recoverable once the unlabeled data is used.
- Running EM to convergence was slightly worse than 5 steps (0.879 vs 0.880); the likelihood optimum
  drifts a little away from the label direction, so the supervised initialisation must anchor it.

WHY IT WORKS
Learning curves separate the two data sources cleanly. Holding out 40% of the labeled rows: going
from 750 to 3,000 labeled rows moves AUC 0.862 -> 0.874, while going from 10k to 203k unlabeled rows
moves it 0.811 -> 0.874. The binding constraint is unlabeled sample size, not labels -- which is
exactly what conditional independence predicts: the class-conditional marginals are 200 univariate
densities, and univariate density estimation is where a 203k-row unlabeled pool buys far more than a
5k-row labeled one. That is the whole result: the mixture is identifiable from unlabeled data alone
because 200 independent coordinates each carry a small mean AND scale shift, the labels only need to
break the sign/anchor the solution, and a nonparametric per-feature ratio then captures the
non-Gaussian component shapes.

METHODOLOGY NOTE
An early round of sweeps was contaminated: my memoisation of the per-fold teacher keyed on the first
few training indices, which collided across folds and let validation labels leak in, inflating CV to
~0.904. I caught it because held-out fold-seed variance was implausibly large, re-keyed the cache on
a hash of the full fold index array, and re-ran every sweep. All numbers quoted above are from the
fixed code.

CONFIRMATION SCORER (3 calls)
Call 1, Gaussian EM + kernel-smoothed nonparametric M-step: 0.8791 (CV 0.887).
Calls 2 and 3, final ensemble (call 3 is the same model after monotone probability calibration,
so identical AUC by construction): 0.8855 (CV 0.894). The confirmation scores tracked CV within the
+/-0.025 standard error of a 1,500-row AUC at this prevalence, so I used CV for all tuning and the
scorer only as an independent check -- 1,500 rows cannot resolve the ~0.001-0.005 differences the
tuning decisions turned on.

FINAL MODEL
Refit on all 5,000 labeled rows plus all 203,000 unlabeled rows (transductive: confirmation, transfer
and real_test rows all participate in the unlabeled density estimation, no labels involved).
Predictions are rank-percentiles mapped through a quadratic-in-logit calibration fitted on the
out-of-fold research predictions, so they are monotone-equivalent to the model score but read as
probabilities (mean predicted probability on real_test 0.0957 vs a 0.0958 base rate).

DATA STRUCTURE FOUND (all conclusions drawn from the supplied files only)

1. The 200 features are mutually independent, not merely uncorrelated-by-accident: on
   200k rows the largest |pairwise correlation| is 0.060 and the correlation-matrix
   eigenvalues run only 1.12 down to ~0.88. There is no latent factor / block structure,
   so nothing is gained by rotations, PCA or feature grouping. Marginals are near-Gaussian
   (|skew| < 0.34) with uniformly negative excess kurtosis (median -0.51), quantized to 4
   decimals; the apparent "low-cardinality" feature x_165_968dbe5 (428 distinct values in
   200k rows) is just a continuous feature with sd 0.007 hitting the quantization grid.

2. real_test is exactly half synthetic. Counting, per column, how often each value occurs
   inside real_test: precisely 100,000 rows have ZERO features whose value is unique, and
   the other 100,000 average 31 unique-valued features (histogram is smooth, 10..60+).
   That 100,000/100,000 split is the signature of row augmentation by per-column
   resampling from the real rows. research / confirmation / transfer are all real
   (mean 84 unique-valued features per row against the pooled 208k). No row is duplicated
   within or across any split, so there is no label-copying shortcut.
   I built the real-row reference pool (5,000 + 1,500 + 1,500 + 100,000 = 108,000) and
   tested frequency encodings from it (count, count>1, value-masked-by-count). They are
   worth at most +0.001 AUC: because the features are continuous and only quantization
   creates repeats, the value count here is essentially a deterministic function of the
   marginal density and therefore adds nothing beyond x_j itself. I did not use them in
   the final model. The 100k synthetic rows WERE still used, legitimately, as unlabeled
   data for estimating the marginal CDFs (see below).

3. The target is purely additive. A LightGBM boosted on top of the additive model's score
   makes it worse (0.855 vs 0.872), and a LightGBM given the raw features plus the radial
   aggregate only reaches 0.852 on its own. I found no interaction structure anywhere.

4. Each per-feature shape function is essentially a QUADRATIC in the normal score. Fitting
   the quantile-normalised features with an orthonormal Hermite basis and measuring the
   score statistic s_jk = mean_{y=1}[h_k(z_j)] - mean_{y=0}[h_k(z_j)] against its null
   sampling variance gives signal-to-noise variance ratios by order:
      order 1 (linear)    5.20      order 3   0.34
      order 2 (quadratic) 0.91      order 4   0.15   (higher orders: noise)

5. THE MAIN FINDING - a shared radial / dispersion component. The order-2 coefficients are
   not sign-symmetric like the linear ones: their mean across the 200 features is +0.0508
   with t = +15.0 (75% positive), while the order-1 mean is indistinguishable from zero
   (t = -1.3). In other words, on top of one linear direction, positives sit systematically
   FURTHER FROM THE CENTRE of the feature distribution in every coordinate. The single
   aggregate R = mean_j z_j^2 scores AUC 0.696 entirely on its own, with P(y=1) rising
   monotonically 0.032 -> 0.252 across its deciles. The effect is spread over all 200
   features rather than driven by extremes (max_j z_j^2 scores only 0.530), and it is
   exactly quadratic - adding R^2, R^3 or a spline in R does not help, nor does an
   interaction between R and the linear score.

MODEL THAT EXPLOITS IT

  z_j = Phi^-1(F_j(x_j)), F_j = empirical CDF over the pooled 208,000 rows (research +
  confirmation + transfer + real_test features; no labels involved). Because the transform
  is fitted on the pool, z_j ~ N(0,1) exactly, which makes the normalized Hermite
  polynomials h_k an orthonormal basis for the class density ratio and makes the design
  matrix essentially orthogonal - so shrinkage is exactly James-Stein. |z| clipped at 3.

  Per feature j and order k <= 3, take s_jk (above) with null variance v_k, then shrink
  toward the ORDER MEAN instead of toward zero:
      w_jk = mu_k + (s_jk - mu_k) * tau_k^2 / (tau_k^2 + v_k),  score = sum_jk w_jk h_k(z_j)
  Shrinking order 2 toward its large positive mean (i.e. toward the radial component)
  rather than toward zero is worth +0.004 AUC (0.8739 vs 0.8700, seed 42) - that is the
  finding of point 5 paying off directly. Mild per-order gains (1.0, 0.8, 0.6) tuned by CV
  add a further +0.0007. A Gaussian prior clearly beats soft-thresholding (0.869 vs 0.847),
  confirming the effects are DENSE across all 200 features rather than sparse.

  Final prediction = 0.78 * this estimator + 0.22 * a 3-seed LightGBM on [z, R], blended as
  standardized logits. The LightGBM is much weaker alone but decorrelated enough to add a
  consistent ~+0.002.

WHAT THE NUMBERS SAID (5-fold CV on the 5,000 research rows)

  logistic on raw features, tuned C            0.845
  LightGBM, tuned                              0.850
  spline GAM (5 knots) on normal scores        0.863
  per-feature Hermite deg 2, tuned block ridge 0.866
  linear + single global sum z^2               0.867
  EB Hermite deg 3, shrink to zero             0.870      (seed 42)
  EB Hermite deg 3, shrink to order mean       0.875      (seed 42)
  same with |z| clipped at 3, repeated CV 5 seeds  0.8704 +- 0.0035
  + LightGBM blend at w = 0.22                 0.8719 +- 0.0034

CONFIRMATION SCORING

  I used the scorer sparingly and treated it as a sanity check rather than a tuning
  signal: with 1,500 rows and ~144 positives its standard error is about 0.018, well above
  the differences I was choosing between, so all model selection was done on repeated CV
  over the 5,000 research rows. The calls were used to verify that the structural finding
  transfers out of sample, and it does - the linear-only model scored 0.8243 while the
  same estimator with the quadratic/radial component scored 0.8539, a +0.030 gain that
  matches (in fact exceeds) the +0.025 the CV predicted. The final blend scored 0.8583 (call 3 of 20; I stopped there rather than spend calls on differences the scorer cannot resolve).
  The gap between confirmation (~0.85) and CV (~0.87) is within roughly one standard error
  and I saw no distribution shift between splits (max KS statistic 0.05 across all 200
  features, all splits), so I did not adjust the model for it.

FINAL MODEL is retrained on all 5,000 research rows and applied unchanged to transfer.json
and to all 200,000 rows of real_test.csv.

DATA STRUCTURE FOUND
--------------------
200 continuous features, 5000 labelled rows (9.58% positive), 1500 confirmation, 1500
transfer, 200,000 real_test rows. Two structural facts drove everything:

(1) The features are mutually independent. Max |pairwise correlation| over the 19,900
pairs is 0.057 -- exactly the max you expect from pure noise at n=5000. I later re-checked
this *within* each class using EM responsibilities over the 103k unlabelled rows: mean
|corr| was 0.0053 (class 1, ESS 23k, noise floor 0.0066) and 0.0025 (class 0, ESS 99k,
noise floor 0.0032). So conditional independence holds to the measurement limit -- there
are no interactions to find, and the Bayes-optimal model is additive in per-feature terms.
This is why capacity-matched generic models underperform here: an LGBM with 5000 rows
spends its capacity looking for interactions that do not exist.

(2) real_test is not a homogeneous sample. Exactly 100,000 of its 200,000 rows contain
*zero* values that are unique within their column, while the other 100,000 have 16 such
values on average -- a sharp bimodal split with no rows in between. That is the signature
of 100k synthetic rows built by resampling each column independently from the 100k genuine
rows. I therefore treat only the 100k genuine rows as usable unlabelled data.

WHAT I TRIED
------------
Baselines (5-fold CV on research, repeated over 3 seeds): L2 logistic on raw features
0.833, LightGBM stumps 0.836, LightGBM depth-3 0.828, quantile+spline GAM 0.812-0.819.
Heavily-regularised logistic converges to the "independence rule" (diagonal LDA), 0.8400 --
already better than any GBM, consistent with fact (1).

I tested the value-count / uniqueness encoding that fact (2) suggests (counts computed over
pack rows + 100k genuine test rows). Pooling per-feature signed correlations across all
200 features, cells with count==1 showed r=+0.0283 vs r=+0.0307 for count>1 -- a 1.4-sigma
difference, i.e. nothing. Adding counts, log-counts or is-unique indicators to the model
*reduced* CV AUC (0.833 -> 0.811). I dropped this line: the uniqueness structure identifies
which test rows are synthetic, but carries no target signal at this label budget.

TWO THINGS THAT ACTUALLY WORKED
-------------------------------
(a) Class-specific per-feature VARIANCES, not just means. Diagonal LDA (mean shifts only)
gets 0.8400; diagonal QDA (mean + variance shifts, still fully supervised, no unlabelled
data) gets 0.8623. Decomposing the final fitted score, the linear (mean-shift) part alone
scores OOF 0.8618 and the quadratic (variance-shift) part alone scores OOF 0.7352, and the
correlation between the two parts is only 0.117 -- the dispersion signal is largely
independent information, not a restatement of the location signal. Mechanistically:
positives are both shifted and ~2.6% more dispersed per feature (rms log-sd shift 0.0264),
and the size of a feature's variance inflation correlates 0.80 with the size of its mean
shift.

(b) Semi-supervised EM over the 103,000 unlabelled rows (confirmation + transfer + the
100k genuine real_test rows). Because the model is a 2-component mixture of *independent*
per-feature distributions, the mixture is identifiable from unlabelled data alone; the 479
labelled positives only need to anchor which component is which. Fitting mean+variance by
EM lifts 0.8623 -> 0.8853 (raw features) and 0.8909 after rank-gaussianising each feature
against the pooled unlabelled marginal. The unlabelled-size sweep (5k/15k/36k/62k/103k ->
0.871/0.875/0.881/0.888/0.890) shows the gain is genuinely driven by unlabelled volume.

FINAL MODEL: rank-gaussianise every feature against the pooled (label-free) distribution of
research+confirmation+transfer+genuine-real_test rows; fit a diagonal two-component
Gaussian mixture by 8 EM iterations, labelled rows held at their true responsibilities;
score by the log-likelihood ratio; Platt-calibrate to probabilities using out-of-fold
scores. CV 0.8904, confirmation 0.8808.

WHAT DID *NOT* WORK, AND WHY IT IS INFORMATIVE
----------------------------------------------
More flexible density models all made things sharply worse under EM: unconstrained
histogram class-conditionals gave 0.822 (16 bins) down to 0.758 (64 bins); the same model
re-expressed as smoothed per-feature marginal posteriors gave 0.804-0.844; degree-3 and
degree-4 polynomial-logit EM gave 0.841 and 0.807, versus 0.891 for the degree-2 (Gaussian)
case. Even warm-starting the flexible models from the converged Gaussian solution did not
save them. The unlabelled likelihood has good optima that do not correspond to the labelled
classes, and the quadratic restriction is precisely what pins EM to the right latent split.
The lesson is that the semi-supervised gain here is bought by *constraint*, not flexibility.

ATTACKING MY OWN RESULT
-----------------------
The specific worry: my model consumes the confirmation and transfer rows as unlabelled data
and is transductive, so a confirmation AUC of 0.88 could reflect adaptation to those
particular rows rather than a real pattern. Five checks:

1. Transductive contamination. I refit with the 1500 confirmation rows *removed* from the
   unlabelled pool and rescored: 0.8806 vs 0.8808. Parameter cosine-similarity with/without
   them is 0.99988 (mean shifts) and 0.99946 (log-sd shifts). They are 1.5% of the pool and
   contribute essentially nothing. This attack fails.
2. Is the confirmation score even load-bearing? It is not: every modelling decision above
   was made on 5x5-fold CV over research rows, which never enter the unlabelled pool, and
   CV (0.8904) and confirmation (0.8808) agree to within the ~0.015 standard error of an
   AUC on 1500 rows with 144 positives. I used only 4 of 20 scorer calls, and never tuned
   against them.
3. Is the novel ingredient (the variance term) a confirmation-set artifact? No -- it
   replicates on a completely separate row set. Submitting the mean-shift-only score scored
   0.8515 on confirmation vs 0.8808 for the full model, matching the OOF gap
   (0.8618 -> 0.8907) almost exactly. And diagonal QDA beats diagonal LDA (0.8623 vs
   0.8400) with no unlabelled data involved at all.
4. Spurious feature or fold artifact? The signal is diffuse: dropping the 5 strongest
   features costs 0.015 (0.8904 -> 0.8756), dropping 20 leaves 0.825, dropping 50 leaves
   0.733. No feature or handful of features is carrying the result, and the seed-to-seed
   CV spread is 0.0004.
5. Distribution shift onto real_test? Adversarial validation (logistic regression
   discriminating research rows from genuine real_test rows) gives AUC 0.4878 -- they are
   the same distribution. And CV AUC *rises* monotonically as real_test rows are added to
   the unlabelled pool, which they could not do if those rows came from elsewhere.

The attack did not turn up anything that overturns the approach, so I finalised it
unchanged and applied exactly this model to real_test.

REMAINING HEADROOM AND HONEST CAVEATS
-------------------------------------
Simulating 200k rows from the fitted mixture and scoring them with the *true* generating
log-ratio gives AUC 0.8975. I reach 0.8904 out-of-fold, so I am within 0.007 of this model
class's own ceiling; the rest is parameter noise. Consistent with that, post-hoc shrinkage
of either effect vector and rank-ensembling with a raw-space (non-gaussianised) EM both
failed to improve on the plain fit. Getting meaningfully further would need a better
density family, and everything I tried in that direction destabilised EM.

The main caveat on real_test: half of its rows are synthetic column-shuffles with no latent
class structure, and my scores on them have visibly lower dispersion (sd 0.133 vs 0.175 on
genuine rows). If those rows' labels are unrelated to their shuffled features, no model can
rank them and the achievable AUC over all 200,000 rows will be well below 0.89 for reasons
outside my control. I deliberately did not special-case them (e.g. flattening their
predictions): that cannot raise expected AUC if their labels are random, and would throw
away real signal if they are not. The same single model is applied to every row.

DATA / STRUCTURE FINDINGS
5,000 labelled rows, 200 anonymised continuous features, base rate 9.58%. The four
splits (research / confirmation / transfer / real_test, 200k rows) are drawn from the
same distribution: per-feature KS statistics between research and each other split are
all <=0.05 (<=0.023 vs the 200k real_test set), i.e. sampling noise.

1. The features are mutually independent. Max |pairwise correlation| over all 19,900
   pairs is 0.057 (n=5,000 => noise sd 0.014); the correlation-matrix spectrum is flat
   (top eigenvalue 1.44). So there is no latent factor structure to recover.
2. The target is *additive*: logit(y) = sum_j f_j(x_j). I ran a score test of every one
   of the 19,900 products x_i*x_j against the working residual of a fitted additive
   model: max |z| = 3.70 and the empirical sd of the 19,900 z-statistics was 0.88 (i.e.
   *fewer* extreme values than the null predicts). Consistent with this, tree models,
   which can represent interactions, do markedly worse than the additive model
   (LightGBM 0.835 CV / 0.832 confirmation vs 0.881 / 0.856).
3. Each f_j is smooth and roughly cubic. Univariate signal is weak (max univariate AUC
   0.581, median 0.523) but *dense*: essentially all 200 features contribute.
   Deconvolving per-feature coefficients in a per-feature orthonormal polynomial basis
   against a label-permutation null gives true across-feature sd 0.103 (degree 1),
   0.024 (degree 2), 0.028 (degree 3), ~0 (degrees 4-5).
4. THE MAIN FINDING - a shared radial ("outlierness") component. The degree-2
   coefficient has a systematic *positive mean* of 0.031 across all 200 features, on top
   of its 0.024 spread. That is, every feature contributes the same U-shaped, symmetric
   term: rows far from the centre in *any* coordinate are more likely to be positive.
   Because the features are independent this is perfectly additive, which is why no
   interaction test detects it. The consequence is a completely *label-free* predictor:
   standardise each feature using the pooled unlabelled rows and take
   R = mean_j |z_j|^3. R alone has AUC 0.723 on research and 0.725 on confirmation, and
   the positive rate rises monotonically from 2.8% in the bottom decile of R to 28.2% in
   the top decile. p=3 beats p=2 (0.723 vs 0.713) and p=1 (0.678); Gaussianising the
   marginals first *hurts* (0.685), so the effect lives on the raw linear scale, and it
   is not simply "negative log marginal density" (that statistic scores only 0.709).
5. Secondary finding: each feature's degree-1 and degree-3 coefficients are positively
   correlated across features (r = 0.31 vs 0.15 under a permutation null; ~0.36 after
   correcting for attenuation), i.e. the odd part of f_j has a consistent shape and only
   its amplitude varies. Also corr(|degree-1|, degree-2) = 0.23 (null 0.03), so features
   with a stronger linear effect also have a stronger even part.

MODEL
An additive ridge logistic regression built to match that structure:
 - per-feature orthonormal polynomial basis (degrees 1-3), orthonormalised on the pooled
   208k unlabelled+labelled rows (unsupervised, so identical at train and test time);
 - an anisotropic Gaussian prior on each feature's coefficients: scale s1 on degree 1,
   s1*r2 on degree 2, s1*r3 on degree 3, and prior correlation rho between the degree-1
   and degree-3 coefficients (finding 5). This coupling is worth ~+0.003 over a diagonal
   prior (0.8787 vs 0.8756);
 - two weakly-penalised *shared* columns, mean_j z_j^2 and mean_j |z_j|^3, which let the
   common radial component (finding 4) be estimated from all 200 features jointly instead
   of being shrunk 200 separate times. Worth +0.010 in CV and +0.012 on confirmation;
 - the prediction is averaged over 8 near-optimal prior settings rather than the single
   CV argmax (guards against tuning noise), then blended in logit space with weight 0.10
   on a capacity-matched LightGBM (+0.001, consistent across 5 CV seeds), and
   Platt-calibrated on out-of-fold predictions.
Hyper-parameters were chosen by repeated (3-5 seed) stratified 5-fold CV on the 5,000
research rows only.

WHAT THE SCORES SAID (5 scorer calls, none used for model selection)
 1. full model v1 (single prior setting)           confirmation AUC 0.8547
 2. label-free radial statistic mean_j|z_j|^3      confirmation AUC 0.7246  (research 0.7233)
 3. final model (8-setting ensemble + LGBM blend)  confirmation AUC 0.8564  (CV 0.8806)
 4. generic capacity-matched LightGBM              confirmation AUC 0.8319  (CV 0.8349)
 5. final model minus the shared radial columns    confirmation AUC 0.8446  (CV 0.8691)
Every ablation ordering seen in CV reproduced on the held-out confirmation rows.

ATTACKING MY OWN APPROACH
(a) Confirmation-set exploitation: I made only 5 scorer calls and used none of them to
    choose a model, a feature, or a hyper-parameter - all selection was CV on the
    research rows. The confirmation AUC (0.8564) is *below* the CV estimate (0.8806),
    so the confirmation set is not flattering the model.
(b) Coincidental overlap / memorisation: there are no exact duplicate rows between
    research and confirmation, transfer or real_test. Nearest-neighbour distances from
    confirmation rows to research rows (min 15.11, median 16.91) are indistinguishable
    from research-to-research nearest-neighbour distances (min 14.91, median 16.92), so
    there is no near-duplicate channel.
(c) THE ATTACK THAT SUCCEEDED, and what I changed. Ranking features by the fitted
    coefficient magnitude of a model trained on all 5,000 rows and then keeping the top
    100 gave CV AUC 0.8869 - *better* than the full 200-feature model (0.8791). Taken at
    face value that says the signal is concentrated and I should be selecting features.
    It is an artifact: the ranking was computed with the held-out folds visible. Redoing
    the selection strictly inside each training fold gives 0.8629 / 0.8689 / 0.8746 /
    0.8774 for top-80 / 100 / 130 / 160 - all *worse* than using all 200, improving
    monotonically toward the full model. Adaptive per-feature reweighting (ARD-style,
    gamma = 0.3-1.0) and elastic-net sparsity (l1_ratio 0.2-0.5) also both hurt. So I
    dropped feature selection entirely and kept the dense ridge; the "signal is dense"
    claim survives only because I checked it this way.
(d) Is the radial finding itself spurious? It cannot be a fold or tuning artifact: the
    statistic mean_j |z_j|^3 has zero fitted parameters (the standardisation uses the
    pooled *unlabelled* rows), and it scores 0.7233 on research and 0.7246 on the sealed
    confirmation rows. The corresponding model ablation replicates externally too
    (+0.0118 on confirmation vs +0.010 in CV).
(e) Residual concern I could not fully eliminate: the CV margin over the generic
    LightGBM baseline (+0.046) is larger than the confirmation margin (+0.0245). Both
    are consistent given a ~+/-0.02 standard error on a 1,500-row AUC and the comparison
    on confirmation is paired, but the shrinkage is the direction you would expect if my
    CV number carries roughly 0.005-0.01 of optimism from tuning five prior
    hyper-parameters on the same 5,000 rows. I mitigated this by averaging over eight
    near-optimal settings instead of the CV argmax, and by keeping every component that
    survives only structural, not numerical, justification. I would expect the sealed
    transfer/real_test AUC to land near 0.855-0.870 rather than 0.88.
